questions.q: What is the accounting equation?
questions.why: Everything the business owns is financed by the owner or by others.

questions.q: Which is a liability?
questions.why: A liability is an amount the business owes.

questions.q: Which is the accounting equation?
questions.why: It always balances.

questions.q: A business has assets of $85 000 and liabilities of $23 000. What is the owner's capital?
questions.why: Capital = Assets − Liabilities, so 85 000 − 23 000 = $62 000.

questions.q: The owner takes $500 cash from the business for personal use. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
questions.why: Drawings reduce cash (an asset) and reduce the owner's capital by the same amount, so the equation still balances.

long.q: A trader's business has premises $60 000, inventory $8000, trade receivables $5000, cash at bank $3000, trade payables $6000 and a bank loan of $20 000. Calculate the total assets, the total liabilities and the owner's capital.
scheme: M1: capital = total assets − total liabilities

long.q: Explain the difference between book-keeping and accounting.
scheme: B1: book-keeping is the detailed recording of financial transactions in the books of prime entry and the ledgers
B1: accounting uses those records to prepare financial statements and to analyse and interpret them so the owner can make decisions

long.q: State the effect on assets, liabilities and capital of each transaction: (a) a machine is bought on credit for $4000; (b) the owner pays $10 000 of her savings into the business bank account; (c) a credit supplier is paid $1500 by bank transfer.
scheme: B1: (a) liabilities (trade payables / other payables) increase by $4000; capital unchanged
B1: (b) capital increases by $10 000; liabilities unchanged
B1: (c) liabilities (trade payables) decrease by $1500; capital unchanged

long.q: Apart from the owner, name two users of a sole trader's financial statements and explain why each needs them.
scheme: B1: one user, e.g. a bank or other lender
B1: reason, e.g. to judge whether the business can repay a loan and its interest before lending
B1: a second user, e.g. trade payables (suppliers) / employees / tax authorities / a possible buyer
B1: reason, e.g. suppliers check the business can pay before giving credit; tax authorities check the profit on which tax is charged

long.q: At the start of a week a business had capital of $35 000 and liabilities of $12 000. During the week the owner took $800 cash for personal use and the business bought inventory for $2000 on credit. Calculate the total assets at the end of the week and show that the accounting equation still balances.
scheme: M1: drawings reduce assets (cash) and capital by $800; the credit purchase increases assets (inventory) and liabilities by $2000
A1: capital 34 200 + liabilities 14 000 = $48 200, so it balances

questions.q: Which document is sent by a seller to request payment?
questions.why: A credit note reduces the amount owed, e.g. for returns.

questions.q: In double entry, buying goods on credit is recorded as…
questions.why: Purchases increase (debit); the amount owed to the supplier increases (credit).

questions.q: Which is the book of prime entry for credit sales?
questions.why: Cash sales go in the cash book.

questions.q: A trader pays a credit supplier $400 by cheque. What is the double entry?
questions.why: The amount owed (a liability) falls, so the supplier is debited; the bank balance falls, so bank is credited.

questions.q: Goods with a list price of $2 000 are sold on credit less 10% trade discount. What amount is entered in the sales journal?
questions.why: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice and never recorded in the ledger, so only the net $1 800 is entered.

long.q: State the difference between an invoice and a credit note.
scheme: B1: an invoice is sent by the seller to a credit customer, showing the amount owed for goods sold
B1: a credit note is sent by the seller to reduce the amount owed, e.g. for returned or faulty goods

long.q: Goods with a list price of $3000 are sold on credit to K, less 20% trade discount. K is offered a 5% cash discount for payment within 14 days and pays within that time. Calculate the amount on the invoice and the amount K pays, and state how the cash discount is recorded.
scheme: B1: the $120 is discount allowed: debited to the discount allowed account as an expense and credited to K's account (trade discount is not entered in the accounts)

long.q: State the account to be debited and the account to be credited for each transaction: (a) goods sold on credit to R for $700; (b) goods returned to a credit supplier, T, $150; (c) rent of $500 paid by bank transfer; (d) the owner takes goods costing $200 for her own use.

Name the book of prime entry used to record each of the following: (a) a credit purchase of goods for resale; (b) the purchase of a machine on credit; (c) goods returned by a credit customer; (d) cash sales.

A business keeps petty cash on the imprest system with an imprest of $250. During the month it paid postage $38, cleaning $62, travel $45 and stationery $27. Calculate the balance before restoring the imprest and the amount needed to restore it, and state one advantage of the imprest system.
scheme: A1: amount needed to restore the imprest = $172
B1: advantage, e.g. spending is checked each period because the cashier must show vouchers for the amount reimbursed / the main cash book is freed from many small payments

questions.q: Which error does NOT affect the trial balance?
o: Entry on the wrong side of one account only
questions.why: Commission errors post to the wrong account of the right type; debits still equal credits.

questions.q: A bank reconciliation explains differences between…
o: the cash book and the bank statement
questions.why: Timing differences like unpresented cheques cause them.

questions.q: Which error does not affect the agreement of the trial balance?
o: Entering different amounts on each side
questions.why: Errors of commission, omission, principle, original entry, reversal and complete reversal don't show in the trial balance.

questions.q: A cash book shows a debit (favourable) bank balance of $3 000. The bank statement shows bank charges of $40 not yet in the cash book. What is the updated cash book balance?
questions.why: Bank charges reduce the money in the bank, so they are credited in the cash book: 3 000 − 40 = $2 960.

questions.q: Repairs of $300 to a delivery van were debited to the motor vehicles account. What type of error is this?
questions.why: Revenue expenditure was posted to a non-current asset account, the wrong class of account, which is an error of principle.

long.q: A trader's cash book shows a debit (favourable) bank balance of $2340. Comparing it with the bank statement shows: unpresented cheques $410; amounts paid in but not yet credited by the bank $650; bank charges of $25 not entered in the cash book; and a credit transfer of $180 from a customer not entered in the cash book. Calculate the updated cash book balance and the balance shown on the bank statement.
scheme: M1: bank statement = 2495 + 410 (unpresented cheques) − 650 (amounts not yet credited)

long.q: Name three types of error that do not affect the agreement of the trial balance, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: one type, e.g. error of omission
B1: example, e.g. a credit sale left out of the books completely
B1: a second type, e.g. error of commission / principle
B1: example, e.g. a payment by L. Shah posted to L. Shaw's account; or a machine purchase debited to purchases
B1: a third type, e.g. original entry / complete reversal / compensating error
B1: example, e.g. an invoice for $560 entered everywhere as $650; or bank debited and rent credited for rent paid

long.q: A trial balance had debit totals of $48 650 and credit totals of $48 200, and the difference was entered in a suspense account. Two errors were then found: the sales journal had been undercast by $300; and discount received of $150 had not been posted to the discount received account. Calculate the suspense account balance and state the entries that correct each error.
scheme: B1: suspense = 48 650 − 48 200 = $450, entered on the credit side
B1: error 1: debit suspense $300, credit sales $300
B1: error 2: debit suspense $150, credit discount received $150
B1: 450 − 300 − 150 = 0, so the suspense account is cleared

long.q: From the following, calculate the closing balance of a sales ledger control account and state one use of the account: opening trade receivables $12 400; credit sales $36 800; sales returns $1200; receipts from credit customers $33 500; discounts allowed $700; irrecoverable debts written off $400.
scheme: B1: use, e.g. it checks the arithmetic of the sales ledger / helps locate errors / gives a quick total of trade receivables

long.q: The purchase of a computer for office use, costing $900, was debited to the purchases account. Name the type of error, explain its effect on the profit for the year and on the statement of financial position (ignore depreciation), and state the entry to correct it.
scheme: B1: cost of sales is overstated, so gross profit and profit for the year are understated by $900
B1: non-current assets (office equipment) are understated by $900
B1: correction: debit office equipment $900, credit purchases $900

questions.q: A machine costs $10 000, lasts 5 years and has no residual value. What is straight-line depreciation per year?
questions.why: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life = 10 000 ÷ 5.

questions.q: Prepaid expenses are shown as…
questions.why: They are paid in advance for a future period.

questions.q: Writing off an irrecoverable debt…
questions.why: It is an expense in the income statement.

questions.q: Inventory items: A cost $50, NRV $40; B cost $30, NRV $45. At what value should inventory be shown?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some compared total cost with total NRV. Apply lower of cost and NRV to each item: 40 + 30 = $70.

questions.q: Annual rent is $6 000. During the year the business paid $5 500. What rent expense is charged in the income statement?
questions.why: The accruals principle charges the full year's cost of $6 000; the unpaid $500 is shown as an accrued expense (a current liability).

long.q: A van cost $12 000 and is expected to last 5 years, with a residual value of $2000. Calculate the annual depreciation using the straight-line method and the net book value after 2 years.
scheme: A1: net book value after 2 years = $8000

long.q: A business buys a new machine. State whether each item is capital expenditure or revenue expenditure: (a) the price of the machine; (b) the delivery charge for the machine; (c) repairs to the machine two years later; (d) wages of the machine operator.
scheme: B1: (b) capital expenditure (a cost of getting the asset ready for use)

long.q: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a business paid rent of $5400; the annual rent is $6000. On 1 April 2025 it paid insurance of $1560 covering the 13 months to 30 April 2026. Calculate the rent and insurance expenses for the income statement and state how the year-end differences are shown in the statement of financial position.
scheme: B1: rent accrued (owing) of 6000 − 5400 = $600 shown as a current liability
A1: insurance prepaid of $120 shown as a current asset

long.q: A shop has 50 identical items in inventory, each costing $80. Ten of them are damaged; they can be sold for $90 each after repairs costing $25 each. Calculate the value of the inventory and explain why the damaged items are valued as they are.
scheme: M1: net realisable value of a damaged item = 90 − 25 = $65
B1: inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (prudence), so damaged items at $65, not $80

long.q: At the year-end trade receivables are $24 000, before writing off $1000 owed by a customer who has become bankrupt. The provision for doubtful debts is to be 4% of the remaining trade receivables; last year's provision was $700. Calculate the amounts charged in the income statement and the net trade receivables in the statement of financial position, and give a reason for keeping the provision.
scheme: B1: irrecoverable debt of $1000 charged as an expense
A1: increase in provision = 920 − 700 = $220 charged as an expense
B1: reason: prudence, so that assets and profit are not overstated by debts that may not be paid

questions.q: Revenue $50 000, cost of sales $30 000. What is gross profit?
questions.why: Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales.

questions.q: Cost of sales is calculated as…
questions.why: It is the cost of the goods actually sold in the period.

questions.q: A club buys new furniture. Where is this shown?
o: Statement of financial position as a non-current asset
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some put the furniture in the income and expenditure account; it is capital expenditure.

questions.q: Gross profit is $32 000, expenses are $19 000 and rent received is $1 500. What is the profit for the year?
questions.why: Profit for the year = gross profit + other income − expenses = 32 000 + 1 500 − 19 000 = $14 500.

questions.q: In a partnership's financial statements, where is interest on partners' capital shown?
o: Statement of financial position as a current liability
Trading account as part of cost of sales
questions.why: Interest on capital is a share of profit to the partners, not a business expense, so it goes in the appropriation account.

long.q: Revenue was $80 000. Opening inventory was $6000, purchases $50 000 and closing inventory $8000. Calculate the cost of sales and the gross profit.

A trader does not keep full records. Her capital was $40 000 at the start of the year and $47 000 at the end. During the year she took drawings of $9000 and paid in additional capital of $5000. Calculate the profit for the year.
scheme: M1: add drawings $9000 and subtract capital introduced $5000

long.q: A sports club received subscriptions of $6400 during the year. This included $300 owed from the previous year and $250 paid in advance for next year. At the year-end members still owed $150 for the current year. No subscriptions had been paid in advance in the previous year. Calculate the subscriptions income for the year for the income and expenditure account.
scheme: M1: subtract the $300 that belongs to the previous year
M1: subtract the $250 paid in advance for next year
M1: add the $150 still owing for the current year

long.q: A manufacturer has: opening inventory of raw materials $4000, purchases of raw materials $30 000, closing inventory of raw materials $5000, direct labour $22 000, factory overheads $12 000, opening work in progress $3000 and closing work in progress $2500. Calculate the prime cost and the production cost of goods completed.
scheme: M1: cost of raw materials consumed = 4000 + 30 000 − 5000 = $29 000
M1: add factory overheads $12 000, add opening and subtract closing work in progress

long.q: A limited company has 200 000 ordinary shares of $1 each. Its retained earnings at the start of the year were $46 000 and its profit for the year was $84 000. It paid ordinary dividends of $30 000 and transferred $10 000 to the general reserve. Calculate the retained earnings at the end of the year and the dividend per share.
scheme: M1: subtract dividends $30 000 and the transfer to general reserve $10 000

questions.q: Gross profit $20 000 on revenue $80 000. What is the gross margin?
A quick (acid test) ratio excludes…
questions.why: Inventory may be slow to turn into cash.

questions.q: What does the current ratio measure?
o: Whether a business can pay its short-term debts
questions.why: Current assets ÷ current liabilities.

questions.q: Revenue is $120 000 and profit for the year is $18 000. What is the profit margin?
questions.why: Profit margin = profit for the year ÷ revenue × 100 = 18 000 ÷ 120 000 × 100 = 15%.

questions.q: Cost of sales is $60 000 and average inventory is $7 500. What is the rate of inventory turnover?
questions.why: Rate of inventory turnover = cost of sales ÷ average inventory = 60 000 ÷ 7 500 = 8 times a year.

long.q: A trader has current assets of $18 000 and current liabilities of $12 000. Calculate the current ratio and comment on it.
scheme: B1: comment, e.g. the business can cover its short-term debts, though below the 2 : 1 often suggested

long.q: A trader's opening inventory was $7000 and closing inventory $9000. Cost of sales for the year was $96 000. Calculate the rate of inventory turnover and suggest one way the trader could improve it.
scheme: B1: improvement, e.g. hold less inventory / order smaller amounts more often / increase sales with promotions or lower prices

long.q: A business had revenue of $150 000, profit for the year of $18 000 and capital employed of $120 000. Calculate the profit margin and the return on capital employed (ROCE).

A business's credit sales for the year were $73 000 and its trade receivables at the year-end were $8000. It allows customers 30 days' credit. Calculate the trade receivables turnover in days (use 365 days) and comment on the result.
scheme: B1: comment: customers take 10 days longer than the 30 days allowed, so credit control is weak and cash comes in more slowly (e.g. send reminders, offer cash discounts)

long.q: A business has inventory $14 000, trade receivables $6000, bank $2000 and current liabilities of $11 000. Calculate its liquid (acid test) ratio and explain why this ratio may be a better test of liquidity than the current ratio.
scheme: B1: inventory is left out because it may take time to sell, or may not sell at its book value, so it is not quickly turned into cash
B1: comment: below 1 : 1, so the business may struggle to pay its current liabilities as they fall due

questions.q: Which principle says revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash is received?
questions.why: Income and expenses are matched to the period they relate to.

questions.q: Prudence means…
questions.why: Accountants shouldn't anticipate gains, but should provide for likely losses.

questions.q: Which concept says a business records assets at cost, not what they'd fetch today?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many could name prudence but struggled to suggest another reason.

questions.q: A business keeps using straight-line depreciation every year instead of switching methods to make profit look higher. Which principle is it following?
questions.why: Consistency means using the same methods from year to year so that results can be compared fairly.

questions.q: The owner pays her home electricity bill from the business bank account. The bookkeeper records it as drawings, not as a business expense. Which principle is applied?
questions.why: The business is treated as separate from its owner, so the owner's private spending is drawings, not a business cost.

long.q: Explain the business entity principle and give one example of how it is applied.
scheme: B1: the business is treated as separate from its owner, so only business transactions are recorded
B1: example, e.g. the owner's personal bills paid from the business bank account are recorded as drawings, not as business expenses

long.q: A trader has inventory that cost $5000. She expects to sell it for $8000 and wants to value it at $8000 in her statement of financial position. Name the principle that prevents this and explain how the inventory should be valued.
scheme: B1: profits must not be anticipated: the gain is only recognised when the goods are sold, and assets must not be overstated
B1: inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, so $5000

long.q: At the end of its financial year a business owes $420 for electricity used in the last two months. Explain how the matching (accruals) principle applies to this bill.
scheme: B1: expenses are matched to the period in which they are used / incurred, not when they are paid
B1: so the $420 is added to the electricity expense in this year's income statement
B1: and shown as an accrued expense (a current liability) in the statement of financial position

long.q: A business switches its depreciation method each year to whichever gives the higher profit. Name the principle this breaks and explain why it matters to users of the financial statements.
scheme: B1: the same accounting methods should be used from one period to the next
B1: otherwise profits are not comparable between years and can be manipulated, misleading users

long.q: Explain two of the objectives that financial statements should meet so that they are useful to their users.
scheme: B1: one objective, e.g. relevance / reliability / comparability / understandability
B1: explained, e.g. relevance: information helps users make decisions and is available in time
B1: explained, e.g. comparability: users can compare with other years and other businesses because methods are consistent; reliability: free from error and bias
